planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall; stake and train young growth to develop the cascading framework.

directions: This uncommon weeping form of black elderberry develops arching, pendulous branches clothed in rich green pinnate foliage, forming an umbrella-like canopy when staked and trained to a central leader. In early summer it produces the same abundant, lacy, creamy-white flower clusters as the species, followed by heavy crops of glossy blue-black fruit. Because the weeping habit depends on training, stake young plants to a desired height and remove any upright reversion shoots. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for best flowering and fruit set.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil; also sold under the synonym 'Heterophylla'.

directions: This striking and unusual form of black elderberry carries leaves dissected into extremely narrow, thread-like leaflets, reduced almost to their midveins, giving the whole shrub a delicate, feathery texture quite unlike the broader cut-leaf 'Laciniata'. Creamy-white flower clusters appear in early summer and are followed by black fruit, though the finely cut foliage is the main ornamental draw. Grow in full sun to partial shade in evenly moist, well-drained soil, and prune hard in late winter to encourage fresh, strongly dissected new growth. Best used as a textural accent or specimen where its fine, lacy outline can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; site where its narrow columnar form fits tight landscape spaces.

directions: A Proven Winners ColorChoice introduction, Laced Up combines a strikingly narrow, fastigiate habit with lacy, near-black dissected foliage on broomstick-straight upright stems. Hundreds of small pink flowers open along the columnar branches in early summer, contrasting with the dark leaves, and will set black fruit if a compatible elderberry such as Black Lace is planted nearby for pollination. Its tight, vertical profile of only a few feet in width makes it useful for narrow garden spaces where a full-spreading elderberry would not fit. Grow in full to partial sun in evenly moist, well-drained soil; it tolerates clay and is drought-tolerant once established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; foliage color develops best in cooler climates.

directions: A Proven Winners ColorChoice selection, Pink Pony pairs dark purple-black foliage with pale pink flower clusters in early summer, which deepen to burgundy-black fruit when cross-pollinated by a compatible elderberry. Its dense, lush, well-branched habit is more refined than many older black-leaf elderberries, giving it good presence in both containers and mixed borders. Foliage color is most intense where summers are cool; in hot climates the leaves may stay predominantly green. Grow in part sun to full sun in moist, well-drained soil, pruning immediately after flowering since it blooms on old wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, well-drained soil.

directions: The cut-leaf counterpart of American elderberry, Acutiloba bears deeply divided, feathery leaflets that are more graceful and finer-textured than the European cut-leaf forms, owing to their longer, more dissected lobes. It still produces the species' flat clusters of white flowers in summer followed by purple-black fruit, but is grown primarily for its soft, airy foliage texture. An uncommon selection best sited at woodland's edge or in a mixed shrub border where its fine texture can offset bolder-leaved neighbors. Grow in full sun to light shade in moist, fertile soil, and cut back hard in late winter to maximize fresh, well-dissected new growth.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring; exceptionally cold-hardy and suited to far-northern elderberry production.

directions: Selected from wild stands growing along the Mattawamkeag River in Aroostook County, Maine, this broad, vigorous, multi-stemmed shrub was chosen for its consistently high yields of tasty purple-black berries under cold, short-season conditions. It carries the typical flat-topped clusters of creamy white flowers in early summer, ripening to heavy fruit clusters by late summer. Rated for USDA zone 3, it is among the most cold-hardy named American elderberry selections available, making it a strong choice for northern homesteads and orchards. Plant with another elderberry cultivar nearby to improve pollination and fruit set.
sources: Maine Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association (MOFGA)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring; pair with a second cultivar such as Korsør or Haschberg for heavier fruit set.

directions: Bred in Denmark and now grown commercially across northern Europe, Allesø is a high-yielding fruiting elderberry valued for its dark green foliage, large clusters of creamy white flowers in May, and heavy sets of jet-black berries on red stems that ripen in September. It is one of the most productive European elderberry cultivars for juice, wine, and syrup production, though its anthocyanin content runs lower than some other Danish selections. Partially self-fertile, it bears more heavily when a second cultivar is planted nearby, and begins cropping within two to three years of planting. Grow in half-day to full sun in well-drained soil; it is largely untroubled by pests or disease.
sources: Aarhus University (Plant Breeding) elderberry variety trials
